title: WHY DID ISRAEL CARRY TWELVE STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN?
paragraphs:
WHY DID ISRAEL CARRY TWELVE STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN?
They Were Carrying More Than Stones. They Were Carrying Evidence That the God Who Brought Them Through Must Never Be Forgotten.
Imagine being the man who had to carry one.
The river is behind you now.
Your clothes carry the smell of the Jordan. Your feet have touched ground that should have been underwater. Your heart is still trying to understand what your eyes have just witnessed.
And there is a stone on your shoulder.
Heavy.
Awkward.
Pulled from the middle of a river where, moments before, nobody should have been able to stand.
You might have wondered why God wanted you to carry it.
After everything He had just done, why a stone?
Why twelve of them?
Why make twelve men go back toward the place everyone else was leaving?
The answer reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
Because God knew something about the human heart.
We forget.
We forget prayers that were answered once the crisis passes.
We forget doors God opened after we become comfortable inside the room.

We forget how desperately we cried when our marriage was breaking, when the diagnosis frightened us, when money disappeared, when temptation had us by the throat, when grief made getting out of bed feel like an act of war.
We remember the pain.
Then God carries us through it...
and eventually we can even forget the Deliverer.
That is why the stones matter.

Joshua 4 opens immediately after Israel crosses the Jordan. God commands Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe, and have each man take a stone from the middle of the river, from the place where the priests bearing the ark had stood firmly. They were to carry those stones to the place where Israel camped.
Not eleven.
Not thirteen.
Twelve.
One corresponding to each tribe of Israel.
This was not merely one man's testimony.
God was marking what He had done for His covenant people.
And then Scripture tells us why.
The stones were to become a sign.
The Hebrew of Joshua 4:6 contains the words:
“לְאוֹת בְּקִרְבְּכֶם”
le’ot beqirbekhem
In context: “for a sign among you.”
Then comes the question God expected future children to ask:
“מָה הָאֲבָנִים הָאֵלֶּה לָכֶם”
Mah ha’avanim ha’elleh lakhem?
“What do these stones mean to you?”
That last idea matters.
Not merely, “What are those rocks?”
What do they mean to you?
There was supposed to be a story attached to them.
A child would see the stones.
Curiosity would become a question.
The question would become testimony.
The testimony would point to the LORD.
And another generation would hear that the God their fathers worshiped was not an imaginary God their ancestors invented to survive difficult times.
He had acted.
He had delivered.
He had made a way where there was no way.
The Hebrew word used in Joshua 4:7 is especially beautiful:
“לְזִכָּרוֹן”
lezikkaron
“For a memorial.”
The noun zikkaron carries the idea of remembrance or memorial. These stones were not magical. Israel was not commanded to worship them. They possessed no spiritual power in themselves.
They pointed beyond themselves.
That distinction matters.
The stones were evidence designed to provoke remembrance.
Look at them...
and remember Him.
Remember where you were.
Remember what stood in front of you.
Remember what God did.
Remember who brought you through.
Because the greatest danger after crossing the river may not always be the enemy waiting ahead.
Sometimes it is forgetting the God who brought you across.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
There was a season when you prayed differently.
You weren't casual then.
You weren't checking your phone every thirty seconds.
You weren't trying to sound spiritual.
You were desperate.
“Jesus, please.”
That was almost the entire prayer.
You promised God that if He brought you through, you would never forget.
Then somehow...
life became normal again.
The tears dried.
The emergency ended.
The relationship survived—or perhaps God gave you strength when it didn't.
The bill got paid.
The temptation loosened its grip.
The funeral passed.
The depression lifted enough for light to enter the room again.
The door opened.
You survived what you once thought would destroy you.
And somewhere between deliverance and comfort, your memory became shorter.
Maybe that is why you needed to encounter twelve stones today.
Because some of us are asking God for another miracle while standing beside forgotten evidence of His faithfulness.
Israel's Jordan crossing itself was deliberate covenant history.
Joshua later tells the people that the LORD dried up the Jordan just as He had dried up the sea before the previous generation.
The God of the Exodus was still the God of Israel.
The generation had changed.
God's faithfulness had not.
That is breathtaking.
The fathers had a sea.
Their children had a river.
Different obstacle.
Same faithful God.
Your testimony does not have to look like somebody else's testimony for Jesus Christ to be the same Lord.
Someone else's Red Sea does not invalidate your Jordan.
Someone may have been delivered instantly while your healing has taken years.
Someone may testify about a marriage restored while your testimony is that Christ held you together after the marriage ended.
Someone may tell how God spared a loved one's life while you still visit a grave.
Biblical faith does not require us to pretend every story ends the way we wanted.
Sometimes the miracle is deliverance from the fire.
Sometimes the testimony is that Christ remained faithful while we walked through it.
The stones were never saying, “God will make your life painless.”
They were saying:
Do not forget who brought you here.
And notice where the stones came from.
The middle.
Not the riverbank.
Not somewhere safe nearby.
God told them to take stones from the place where the priests' feet had stood in the Jordan.
They carried evidence out of the place they had passed through.
There is something painfully familiar about that.
Sometimes what you carry after suffering feels heavy because it came from the deepest part of the crossing.
A scar.
A memory.
A testimony you never wanted.
A tenderness you did not have before grief.
A compassion born from your own failure.
A humility produced when your secret sin finally broke you.
A dependence on Christ that comfortable Christianity never taught you.
Be careful here: Scripture does not teach that every wound is itself good or that every tragedy was secretly something pleasant.
But Scripture repeatedly shows us a God powerful enough to redeem what evil, suffering, sin, and death meant to destroy.
And nowhere is that clearer than at the cross.
Because eventually the biblical story brings us to something far more scandalous than twelve stones beside the Jordan.
It brings us to a cross outside Jerusalem.
Christianity does not center on humanity climbing its way toward God.
It centers on God coming to sinners in Jesus Christ.
Christ crucified.
The sinless One bearing sin.
The righteous One suffering for the unrighteous.
The Son of God entering death...
and rising again.
The cross looked like defeat.
God turned it into the proclamation of redemption.
The tomb looked final.
On the third day, it became empty.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that you can rewrite yourself.
Jesus saves sinners.
Jesus forgives the repentant.
Jesus receives the broken.
Jesus transforms those who come to Him in faith.
Jesus does not merely improve the old story.
He gives new life.
Maybe your past contains things you desperately wish you could erase.
Sexual sin.
Addiction.
Pride.
Adultery.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
A destroyed relationship.
Religious hypocrisy.
Years of pretending.
A secret nobody at church knows.
Words you cannot take back.
People you wounded.
Promises you broke.
Perhaps you have learned how to smile while carrying stones nobody else can see.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
Grace is greater precisely because sin is serious.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity needed motivational encouragement.
We needed reconciliation with God.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed rescue.
We needed a Savior.
And at Calvary, Christ paid a price we could never pay for ourselves.
So repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Him.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can cleanse you.
Maybe your deepest shame does not have to become the final sentence over your life.
Maybe the thing Satan keeps using to whisper, “Look what you did,” can eventually become the place from which you answer, “Look what Christ has done.”
Not because sin becomes beautiful.
Because grace is.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not editing the ugly chapters.
Not calling darkness light.
It is looking directly at the truth of human sin and then looking higher at the cross of Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Joshua's stones also reveal something desperately needed in our homes.
God expected children to ask questions.
Think about that.
The memorial was built with the next generation in mind.
“When your children ask...”
Tell them.
God's mighty works were not supposed to die inside the memories of those who experienced them.
Parents were expected to speak.
Children were expected to hear.
Faithfulness was supposed to become testimony.
And maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
What will your children know about what God has done in your life?
Do they know what Jesus rescued you from?
Do they know why you worship?
Do they know about the prayer God answered when nobody else knew you were praying?
Do they know there were nights you nearly gave up?
Do they know why certain Bible verses make your voice shake?
Do they know the person you were before Christ began changing you?
Or will they inherit your possessions without inheriting your testimony?
We carefully preserve photographs.
Documents.
Graduation certificates.
Jewelry.
Property.
Passwords.
Bank accounts.
Family recipes.
But sometimes we fail to preserve the stories of God's faithfulness.
Tell them.
Tell your children.
Tell your grandchildren.
Tell the young believer who assumes you have always been strong.
Tell the person who thinks their failure has disqualified them forever.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them you were not always okay.
Tell them about the river.
Tell them about the nights.
Tell them about the tears.
Tell them about the sin Christ confronted.
Tell them about repentance.
Tell them about mercy.
Tell them about the prayers that seemed unanswered and how God remained worthy anyway.
Tell them about the moment you discovered Christianity was not about performing religious goodness but about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Build memorials with your words.
Because somebody else's faith may be strengthened by remembering what God did when you thought your story was over.
And Joshua 4 goes even further.
The memorial was not only about Israel remembering.
Joshua says God acted so that “all the peoples of the earth” would know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, and so Israel would fear the LORD continually.
The miracle had a missionary horizon.
God's greatness was meant to be known.
That changes how we think about testimony.
Your testimony is not ultimately about making you impressive.
It is about making Christ known.
If God rescued you from addiction, Christ is the hero.
If He restored you after failure, Christ is the hero.
If He carried you through grief, Christ is the hero.
If He convicted you of hidden sin, Christ is the hero.
If He gave you strength to confess, repent, forgive, reconcile, endure, or begin again...
Christ is the hero.
The stones did not say, “Look how courageous Israel was.”
They said, in effect:
Look what the LORD did.
And perhaps that is why some testimonies never reach the people who desperately need them.
We are afraid of what people will think if they discover where our stones came from.
We want resurrection without admitting there was a tomb.
We want grace without admitting there was guilt.
We want testimony without vulnerability.
We want people to know we crossed the Jordan without letting them know how impossible the river once looked.
But somebody is still standing where you once stood.
Someone scrolling Facebook tonight thinks God could never forgive them.
Someone is fighting pornography secretly.
Someone's marriage is collapsing quietly.
Someone goes to church every Sunday while wondering whether anybody would still love them if the truth came out.
Someone has been away from Jesus so long that returning feels embarrassing.
Someone believes their failure is stronger than Christ's mercy.
They do not need you pretending you have never needed grace.
They need the truth.
You were a sinner too.
You still need grace every day.
And Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
So maybe your “stone” needs to speak.
Maybe your testimony needs to leave the private riverbank.
Maybe someone needs to hear:
“I almost gave up too.”
“I wandered too.”
“I failed too.”
“I hid too.”
“I cried too.”
“But Jesus met me there.”
That does not make you the Savior.
It points people toward the One who is.
This is why sharing Gospel-centered truth matters when it comes from the right motive.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Christ—not a commercial transaction.
But when Christ has given us truth worth remembering, love can move us to help put that truth in front of somebody else.
So if this article made you remember your own Jordan, don't let it disappear into your feed.
Not as a religious performance.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
If you are carrying something heavy and need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ is still working in parts of your life nobody else sees, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God and from yourself, comment, “no more hiding.”
If you have crossed a Jordan you thought would destroy you, tell us what Jesus has done.
Your comment may become somebody else's reason to keep seeking Christ tonight.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider staying close.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and voluntary generosity can be one expression of that worship.
Not because an algorithm is worthy of your obedience.
Because someone in your circle may need to remember that there is still a God who brings people through impossible places.
And after everything else in Joshua 4, perhaps this is the detail that should stay with us.
The river started flowing again.
Joshua 4:18 says that after the priests carrying the ark came up from the Jordan and their feet reached dry ground, the waters returned to their place and overflowed their banks as before.
Think about that.
The path disappeared.
Someone arriving later could look at that raging river and say:
“There was never a road there.”
And Israel could point toward twelve stones.
Yes.
There was.
We walked through it.
God made the way.
That is what testimony does.
Years later, people may look at you and never understand what Jesus brought you through.
They will see you worship but not know the night you almost walked away.
They will see the marriage but not know the war it survived.
They will see the smile but not know the grief behind it.
They will see the ministry but not know the repentance.
They will see the faith but not know how many times you cried, “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.”
They will see dry clothes.
You will remember the river.
So keep the stones.
Not to worship your past.
Not to glorify your pain.
Not to romanticize your sin.
Keep them in memory so that when the enemy tells you God has abandoned you, you can remember His faithfulness.
Keep them so your children can ask.
Keep them so your grandchildren can hear.
Keep them so strangers can discover that the hand of the LORD is mighty.
Keep them until every scar becomes an opportunity to point beyond yourself.
And when someone eventually looks at your life and asks...
“What do these stones mean?”
Tell them.
Tell them about the river.
Tell them about your failure.
Tell them about your fear.
Tell them about the night you thought everything was finished.
But do not stop there.
Tell them about the cross.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them about repentance.
Tell them about forgiveness.
Tell them about mercy you did not deserve.
Tell them about Jesus Christ.
Because the most unforgettable memorial is not the stone you carried out of the river.
It is the Savior who carried you through it.
The river may have covered the road again—but the stones still remember where God made a way.
